The Iberian ribbed newt, Pleurodeles waltl, is a notably large urodele inhabiting temporary and permanent water bodies across the Iberian Peninsula and northern Morocco. Field surveys tracking marked individuals have documented that reproduction is tightly linked to thermal conditions, with a maximum laying rate estimated at 200 eggs per year [Ri = 200 eggs per year] when water temperatures remain stable at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Females deposit their clutches in multiple batches throughout the extended breeding season, a reproductive strategy likely shaped by the unpredictability of Mediterranean pond hydroperiods. Newly hatched larvae weigh approximately 0.18 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.18 grams], an initial mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves provisioned within each egg, which has a diameter of roughly 7 millimeters. This modest size at emergence, combined with a relatively short time to independence, appears to be an adaptation to rapid larval development in ephemeral aquatic habitats where desiccation risk is high.

Larval development proceeds at a pace governed primarily by water temperature. At a constant water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the larval period extends 138 days since birth , during which the aquatic tadpole undergoes dramatic morphological transformation including limb bud development and tail resorption. At the onset of metamorphic climax, individuals typically reach a wet weight of 4.4 grams , a size that appears necessary to successfully transition from the gill-breathing larval stage to the post-metamorphic juvenile form. This value is consistent with observations from natural populations in central Spain, where metamorphling body mass rarely falls below this threshold, suggesting a minimum energetic requirement for completing the body plan reorganisation characteristic of amphibian metamorphosis.

Sexual maturation in Pleurodeles waltl is a comparatively slow process relative to many other European salamandrids. Under captive conditions with a constant thermal regime of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], individuals typically attain puberty after 396 days since birth [tp = 396 days since birth]. At this developmental milestone, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 18 grams [Wwp = approximately 18 grams], a body mass that signals the onset of gonad maturation and gametogenesis. In the wild, this age may be delayed by several months due to seasonal fluctuations in prey availability and lower average winter temperatures, meaning first amplexus is often deferred until the second or third spring following hatching. The attainment of this critical body mass appears to be a key physiological trigger, as laboratory studies have found that individuals smaller than 18 grams rarely exhibit secondary sexual characteristics such as the development of the distinctive rib tips used in defensive displays.

Adult body size exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining substantially larger asymptotic masses than males. The ultimate wet weight for females has been recorded at 62 grams [Wwi = 62 grams], whereas males reach a smaller adult mass of 33 grams [Wwi = 33 grams]. This divergence, which corresponds to a roughly two-to-one ratio in favor of females, is likely driven by fecundity selection, as larger females can carry a greater number of yolked oocytes. Field-collected gravid individuals weighing close to the female asymptote have been observed to produce over 300 oocytes in a single breeding season, underscoring the selective advantage of large body size in this species. The smaller male body mass may also facilitate greater mobility during the breeding season, enabling males to locate and court multiple females across the pond environment.

The maximum lifespan of the Iberian ribbed newt under controlled laboratory conditions, when maintained at a stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], has been documented at 19.5 years [am = 19.5 years]. This remarkable longevity, exceptional among western Palearctic urodeles, allows repeated breeding over many seasons and likely buffers the population against occasional years of complete reproductive failure due to drought. Newly hatched individuals emerge after an incubation period of 13 days [ab = 13 days] at the same thermal regime of 18 °C, a relatively brief embryonic duration that minimizes the vulnerability of the yolk-dependent embryos within the gelatinous egg masses to aquatic predators and fungal infections at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. The combination of a short age at birth, an extended juvenile phase, and an exceptionally long adult reproductive window positions Pleurodeles waltl as a classic bet-hedging strategist, investing in longevity to offset the high interannual variability in recruitment success typical of Mediterranean temporary wetlands.
